title: Chain OF Custody
summary: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected a piece of evidence, when and where it was collected, how it was handled and stored, who accessed it afterwards, and how it was transferred between custodians. In digital forensics the evidence is usually a disk image, a memory capture, a mobile extraction, a log export or a set of network captures, and the record takes the form of a custody form supported by artefacts such as write blockers, hash values, sealed storage, signed transfer receipts and case management timestamps. The purpose is to make the evidence defensible: in a disciplinary hearing, a civil dispute, a regulatory investigation or a criminal prosecution, opposing counsel will challenge whether the artefact presented is the same artefact that existed at the scene, and an unbroken chain with matching cryptographic hashes is the standard answer. Chain of custody begins before acquisition with authorisation and scope, continues through the use of validated tools and write blockers, and extends into analysis, where working copies are made and originals remain sealed. Breakpoints - an unexplained gap, a missing signature, an analyst who examined the original without documenting it, storage in an uncontrolled location - do not automatically make evidence inadmissible, but they weaken its weight and can be fatal in the strictest proceedings. Good practice treats custody as a habit rather than as paperwork: hash on acquisition and again on every transfer, log every access, store in access-controlled locations, and never let convenience override the record.
objectives: Explain what chain of custody must record and why each element affects admissibility and evidential weight.
Document the acquisition, transfer, storage and analysis of digital evidence using a defensible custody record.
Apply cryptographic hashing at acquisition and at each transfer to demonstrate that evidence is unaltered.
Use write blockers and validated tooling so that original media is never modified during examination.
Identify common custody breakpoints and assess how each one weakens the evidence in a hearing or investigation.
Coordinate custody handling with legal counsel, HR and law enforcement expectations before collection begins.
Design storage and access controls that keep sealed originals separate from analyst working copies.

beginner.definition: Chain of custody is the written record of who handled a piece of evidence, when, where, and why. For digital evidence, that could be a disk copy, a memory capture, a log export, or a disk image. The record shows every transfer and every person who accessed it. It proves the evidence you present is the same evidence you collected.
beginner.whyItMatters: Evidence only helps if people trust it. In a disciplinary meeting, a lawsuit, or a police case, the other side will ask how you know the files were not changed. A tidy record, with matching fingerprint values called hashes, answers that question. A gap in the record, even an honest one, weakens your case and may make the evidence useless.
howItWorks: Before you touch anything, confirm you have written permission to collect the evidence.
Write down what you took, the exact time, the place, and the device it came from.
Make a copy and never work on the original, so the original stays untouched.
Create a hash, a digital fingerprint, and record it so any later change becomes obvious.
Log every handover with a signature, a date, and the reason for the transfer.
Store the evidence in a locked, access-controlled place and review who opened it.
beginner.example: Imagine handing a sealed hospital sample to a lab. The nurse signs a form, the courier signs it, and the lab signs again on arrival. Every step has a name and a time. If the seal is broken or a signature is missing, the result cannot be trusted. Digital evidence works the same way. The form and the seal are your record.
takeaways: Write down every handover, with a name, a time, and a reason.
Always work on a copy and keep the original sealed and untouched.
Record a hash so any later change to the evidence is easy to spot.
